notes: Male reproductive system: testes (2, kidney-shaped, along the dorsal wall) → vasa deferentia → seminal vesicles → cloaca; no copulatory organ.
Female reproductive system: ovaries (2, lobed, along the dorsal wall) → oviducts (funnel-shaped opening near the kidney) → uterus → cloaca.
Eggs: unfertilised ova are released into the oviducts; the oviduct adds a jelly coat; eggs are deposited in water.
Fertilisation: EXTERNAL; the male mounts the female (amplexus), releases sperm over the eggs as the female releases eggs; fertilisation in water.
Amplexus: male grasps the female behind the ribs (axillary amplexus in Rana) to ensure sperm is released near the eggs.
Development: fertilised egg → zygote → blastula → gastrula → tadpole (larva with gills + tail) → metamorphosis → adult frog.
Economic/ecological importance: pest control (eats insects), indicator of water quality (sensitive to pollution), food in some cultures.
NEB focus: male and female reproductive organs; external fertilisation; amplexus; development.
confusion: Frogs have EXTERNAL fertilisation (in water), NOT internal.
The male does NOT have a copulatory organ; he releases sperm over the eggs during amplexus.
Amplexus: male grasps the female (axillary in Rana, inguinal in some frogs) to coordinate egg and sperm release.
The oviduct adds a jelly coat to the eggs; the jelly protects the eggs in water.
Tadpoles have gills + tail; adults have lungs + no tail (metamorphosis).
The testes are kidney-shaped and lie along the dorsal body wall; the ovaries are lobed and also on the dorsal wall.

enrichedContent.summary: The frog's reproductive system is adapted for external fertilisation in water. The male has two kidney-shaped testes, vasa deferentia, seminal vesicles, and a cloaca (no copulatory organ). The female has two lobed ovaries, oviducts that add a jelly coat, a uterus, and a cloaca. During amplexus, the male grasps the female and both release gametes into the water, where external fertilisation occurs. Development proceeds from the zygote to the tadpole (gills + tail) to the adult frog (lungs, no tail) via metamorphosis. Frogs are ecologically important as pest controllers and water-quality bio-indicators.

Kingdom protista (Gr; protistos, first of all) was proposed by Ernst Haeckel in 1866.

Later, an American taxonomist Robert Harding Whittaker broadly divided all the living beings of this universe into five kingdoms in 1969 basically on the basis of phylogenetic relationship among them.
1 Five kingdom classification Protistans consist of microscopic, single-celled and primitive eukaryotic organisms.
This group includes diverse living organisms that are plant-like, such as golden algae and diatoms, animals like such as Paramecium and Amoeba.
Some of them are both plants and animals like such as Euglena and Astasia and some of them are fungi like such as Fuligo, Protostelium, etc.
